title: Tables, Keys and Constraints
objectives: Describe the relational model in plain terms
Choose primary, foreign and unique keys
Use constraints so the database rejects bad data

cards.title: Facts in rows, rules in the schema
cards.body: A relational database stores data as tables of rows with named, typed columns. Each row states one fact (“order 42 belongs to customer 7”). Keys identify rows and link tables, and constraints let the database itself refuse data that breaks the rules, whatever application wrote it.

cards.title: Misconception: the application already checks this
cards.body: Application checks run in one code path at one moment. Other services, scripts, migrations and concurrent requests bypass them. Two requests can both check “email not taken” and both insert. A unique constraint in the database is the only check that holds for every writer at once.

cards.title: Linking orders to customers
cards.body: A foreign key ties a child row to a parent row and keeps the link valid.
steps: customers(id primary key, email unique not null)
orders(id primary key, customer_id references customers(id), total check (total >= 0))
Inserting an order for customer 999 that does not exist fails
Deleting a customer with orders fails (restrict) or removes them too (cascade), as you choose
An index on orders.customer_id keeps those checks and joins fast

cards.title: Natural or surrogate keys
cards.body: A natural key comes from the data (an email, an ISBN); a surrogate key is generated (an integer sequence or a UUID). Natural keys change in real life: people change email addresses. A common pattern is a surrogate primary key plus a unique constraint on the natural one.

cards.title: Trap: forgetting how NULL behaves
cards.body: NULL means “unknown”, so NULL = NULL is not true, and a column that allows NULL may hold many of them even with a unique constraint (in PostgreSQL unless you ask for NULLS NOT DISTINCT). Mark columns NOT NULL unless missing values are genuinely allowed.

cards.title: Edge case: NULL in a unique column
cards.body: In standard SQL, NULL is not equal to NULL, so a UNIQUE constraint lets many rows hold NULL in that column. PostgreSQL behaves this way by default (version 15 added UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT to change it); SQL Server allows only one NULL in a unique index. If “at most one row without a value” matters, say so explicitly rather than relying on the default.

questions.prompt: Two sign-up requests with the same email arrive at the same moment. What reliably prevents a duplicate account?

choices.label: A unique constraint on the email column
A check in the sign-up handler before inserting
Validating the email format in the browser
A unique index on the users table’s id column

questions.explanation: Only the database sees both inserts and can reject the second.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key from orders.customer_id to customers.id guarantee?

choices.label: Every order points at a customer that exists
Customer ids are never reused
Orders are stored next to their customer
Every customer has at least one order

questions.explanation: Referential integrity: no orphaned child rows.

questions.prompt: Why is an email address a risky primary key?

choices.label: Emails are too long for any index to handle
It can change, and every referencing row would need updating
Primary keys must always be whole numbers
Two users can never share a unique email

questions.explanation: Keys should be stable; use a surrogate key with a unique email.

questions.prompt: What does each row in a well-designed table represent?

choices.label: One fact about one entity or relationship
One request to the API
One screen in the application
One file on disk

questions.explanation: Tables model the domain, not the user interface.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to add orders that belong to customers.

items.label: Create orders with a customer_id column
Create customers with a primary key
Add a foreign key from orders.customer_id to customers.id, choosing restrict or cascade on delete
Index orders.customer_id

questions.explanation: The parent table comes first, then the child table, then the link with its delete rule. The index can be added before or after the foreign key, so both orders are accepted.

questions.prompt: A users table needs a primary key. Users sign in by email and may change it; other tables reference users.

approaches.label: No primary key; look users up by email
Generated surrogate id as the primary key, plus a unique constraint on email

rationaleOptions.label: The unique constraint still blocks duplicate emails
Tables work fine without a primary key
Natural keys avoid an extra column so they are always better
References use an id that never changes

rationaleConflicts.r3: They break when the real-world value changes, cascading updates everywhere.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Without one, duplicates and ambiguous updates creep in and other tables cannot reference rows reliably.

questions.explanation: Stable surrogate keys for references; unique constraints for the natural identifiers.

flashcards.back: A column (or set) that uniquely identifies each row; unique and not null.
A reference that must point at an existing row in another table.
No; the comparison is unknown.

sources.title: E. F. Codd: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (ACM, 1970)

mechanism.title: How the relational model and constraints protect data
steps: Codd’s 1970 paper proposed storing data as relations, sets of tuples, queried by what you want rather than how to find it. SQL tables are close to that: rows with the same columns, no meaningful order, and each row identified by its values.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL. A table may have other candidate keys, which you declare as unique constraints so the database enforces them too. Composite keys (two or more columns together) suit link tables such as order_items(order_id, product_id).

A foreign key says a column’s values must exist in another table’s key. The database checks it on insert and update, and on delete of the parent it applies the rule you chose: restrict or no action (refuse), cascade (delete children), set null or set default.

Check constraints express rules about a row (total >= 0, end_date > start_date). Not-null constraints say a value is required. Constraints run inside the same transaction as the write, so concurrent writers cannot slip past them the way application-side checks can.

SQL uses three-valued logic: comparisons with NULL give “unknown”, which WHERE treats as false. That is why “WHERE x = NULL” finds nothing (use IS NULL), and why NOT IN with a NULL in the list can return no rows at all.
Constraints cost a little on every write, and foreign keys need an index on the referencing column to keep parent deletes and joins fast; PostgreSQL does not create that index automatically.

useWhen: Declare primary keys, foreign keys, unique and check constraints for every rule the data must always obey.
Use surrogate keys for references and unique constraints for natural identifiers.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying only on application code to keep data consistent.
Avoid nullable columns where a value is always required.

rows: No two rows share a value

numbers.title: How often a check-then-insert race hits
assumptions: Sign-ups: 50 per second at peak (illustrative)
Check-then-insert window in the app: 20 ms
Duplicate submissions (double-clicks, retries) of the same email: 1 in 500 sign-ups (illustrative)
steps: Duplicate attempts per second: 50 ÷ 500 = 0.1, so about 360 an hour at peak.
Most retries arrive within a fraction of a second, so many land inside the 20 ms window of the first request.
Without a unique constraint, each one that does becomes a duplicate account to clean up later.
With the constraint, the second insert fails and the app returns “already registered”.
numbers.result: Races that look rare per request happen many times a day at scale; constraints catch every one.

india.title: Codd’s relational model and the PostgreSQL constraint docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: E. F. Codd’s 1970 paper in Communications of the ACM introduced relations, keys and the idea of describing what data you want independently of how it is stored. The PostgreSQL documentation on constraints describes check, not-null, unique, primary key and foreign key constraints, including the delete actions and the advice to index referencing columns.

pitfalls.trap: “We check for duplicates in code, so we don’t need a unique index.”
pitfalls.say: “Concurrent requests both pass that check; I’d add a unique constraint and handle the error.”

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s use the email as the primary key.”
pitfalls.say: “Emails change; I’d use a surrogate id and a unique constraint on email.”

takeaways: Rows state facts; keys identify and link them.
Constraints hold for every writer, unlike application checks.
Foreign keys need an index on the referencing column.
NULL is unknown: use IS NULL and NOT NULL deliberately.

interactive.title: Which insert fails?
interactive.prompt: customers has id primary key and email unique. orders has customer_id referencing customers(id). Customer 7 exists. Which statement is rejected?

choices.label: Insert an order with customer_id 999
choices.feedback: Right: no customer 999 exists, so the foreign key rejects it.

choices.label: Insert an order with customer_id 7
choices.feedback: Customer 7 exists; the reference is valid.

choices.feedback: Many orders per customer is exactly what the design allows.

title: Joins and Grouping, Conceptually
objectives: Predict how many rows a join returns
Choose between inner and outer joins
Explain the logical order of a query with GROUP BY and HAVING

cards.title: Combining and summarising
cards.body: A join combines rows from two tables where a condition matches, such as orders.customer_id = customers.id. Grouping collapses rows that share a value into one row per group, and aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) summarise each group.

cards.title: Worked example: counting rows before you run the join
cards.body: Row counts tell you whether a join result is right.
steps: Assume: 100 customers; 70 have exactly 4 orders each, 30 have none
Inner join customers to orders: 70 × 4 = 280 rows
Left join (keep every customer): 280 + 30 customers with NULL order columns = 310 rows
Group the left join by customer and COUNT(orders.id): 100 rows, 30 of them with count 0
cards.note: Result. 280, 310 and 100 rows. COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(orders.id) would wrongly give the 30 customers a count of 1, because their single NULL-filled row still counts.

cards.title: The logical order of a query
cards.body: SQL is written SELECT first, but it is evaluated in a different logical order.
steps: FROM and JOIN: build the combined rows
WHERE: filter individual rows
GROUP BY: form groups
HAVING: filter groups using aggregates
SELECT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT

cards.title: Inner, left and the rest
cards.body: An inner join keeps only matching pairs. A left (outer) join keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with NULL where nothing matches. Right and full outer joins do the same for the other side or both. A cross join pairs every row with every row, which is rarely what you want.

cards.title: Trap: summing after a fan-out join
cards.body: Joining orders to order_items repeats each order once per item. Summing orders.total over that result counts each order’s total several times. Aggregate each table at its own level first, or sum item amounts instead.

cards.title: Edge case: a WHERE clause that undoes a LEFT JOIN
cards.body: A LEFT JOIN keeps rows with no match, filling the right side with NULL. Adding WHERE right_table.status = 'active' then removes exactly those rows, because NULL = 'active' is not true, so the query behaves like an inner join. Put conditions on the right table in the ON clause when unmatched rows should stay.

questions.prompt: You want every customer, including those with no orders. Which join?

choices.label: customers INNER JOIN orders
customers LEFT JOIN orders
orders LEFT JOIN customers
customers CROSS JOIN orders

questions.explanation: The left join keeps unmatched left rows.

questions.prompt: Which clause can filter on COUNT(*) > 5?

choices.label: HAVING
WHERE
FROM
ON

questions.explanation: WHERE runs before groups exist; HAVING runs after.

questions.prompt: After a left join, a customer with no orders appears once with NULL order columns. What does COUNT(orders.id) give for them?

choices.label: An error
NULL

questions.explanation: COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts the row.

questions.prompt: Revenue doubled after you joined order_items to orders and summed orders.total. Why?

choices.label: Each order’s total repeated once per item row
The join removed orders with no items
SUM ignores NULL totals
GROUP BY sorted the rows twice

questions.explanation: Fan-out joins multiply parent rows.

questions.prompt: Order the logical evaluation of a grouped query.

items.label: ORDER BY and LIMIT
GROUP BY
FROM and JOIN
HAVING
SELECT
WHERE

questions.explanation: Rows, filter, group, filter groups, project, sort and cut.

questions.prompt: 50 authors: 20 have 3 books each, 30 have none. How many rows does authors LEFT JOIN books return?
assumptions: Every author kept
Unmatched authors appear once
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a left join never returns fewer rows than the left table has (here 50), and an inner join would drop the 30 authors without books.

flashcards.back: Inner keeps matches only; left keeps every left row, with NULLs where no match.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs.

mechanism.title: What joins and grouping do to rows
steps: A join is conceptually a filtered pairing: take every combination of rows from the two inputs and keep those where the join condition is true. The database never actually builds every pair; it uses nested loops, hashing or merging (see the query-planning lesson), but the result is defined this way.

Join cardinality follows the relationship. One-to-one keeps row counts; one-to-many repeats the “one” side once per match; many-to-many through a link table can multiply rows quickly. Knowing the expected count is the fastest way to spot a wrong join condition.

Outer joins keep unmatched rows and fill the missing side with NULLs. A WHERE condition on the right table’s columns after a left join (WHERE orders.status = ’paid’) silently turns it back into an inner join, because NULL rows fail the condition; put such conditions in the ON clause instead.

GROUP BY forms one group per distinct combination of grouping columns. Each output column must be either a grouping column or an aggregate. Aggregates ignore NULLs except COUNT(*), and an empty set gives NULL for SUM and AVG but 0 for COUNT.
The logical order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT) explains many rules: you cannot use an aggregate in WHERE, and a column alias defined in SELECT is not visible in WHERE.
Set operations combine whole query results: UNION removes duplicates (costing a sort or hash) while UNION ALL keeps them; INTERSECT and EXCEPT find common and missing rows.

useWhen: Use joins to fetch related data in one query instead of one query per row.
Use GROUP BY with HAVING for summaries such as “customers with more than five orders”.
avoidWhen: Avoid aggregating parent columns after joining to a child table.
Avoid filtering an outer-joined table in WHERE when you meant to keep unmatched rows.

rows: All entities, related data if any

numbers.title: How fast a many-to-many join grows
assumptions: 10,000 orders, 5 items each on average; each item has 3 tags (illustrative)
Query joins orders → items → item_tags
steps: orders ⋈ items: 10,000 × 5 = 50,000 rows.
Adding item_tags: 50,000 × 3 = 150,000 rows.
Summing orders.total over this result would count each order 15 times.
Aggregating tags per item first (or using EXISTS for a filter) keeps the result at 50,000 rows or fewer.
numbers.result: Every one-to-many hop multiplies rows; aggregate at the right level before joining further.

india.title: Joins and aggregates in the PostgreSQL tutorial
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL tutorial introduces joins with a weather and cities example, showing inner and left outer joins and how unmatched rows appear with NULLs, and its aggregate chapter explains why WHERE cannot contain aggregates while HAVING can, because WHERE is applied before groups are formed. The table-expressions chapter defines the evaluation order formally.

pitfalls.trap: “The report is wrong; SQL is unreliable.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check the row count after each join; fan-out usually explains doubled totals.”

pitfalls.trap: “Filter the left join in WHERE.”
pitfalls.say: “That drops the unmatched rows; I’d move the condition into the ON clause.”

takeaways: Joins pair matching rows; one-to-many repeats the parent.
Left joins keep unmatched rows with NULLs.
WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.
COUNT(col) skips NULLs; aggregate before fan-out.

interactive.title: How many rows?
interactive.prompt: customers has 10 rows. 6 customers have 2 orders each; 4 have none. You run customers LEFT JOIN orders ON … WHERE orders.status = ’paid’, and every order is paid.

choices.label: 12 rows: the WHERE drops the 4 customers without orders
choices.feedback: Right: their order columns are NULL, so the condition is not true and the left join behaves like an inner join.

choices.label: 16 rows: 12 matches plus 4 unmatched customers
choices.feedback: That is what you would get with the condition in the ON clause.

choices.label: 10 rows, one per customer
choices.feedback: Joins repeat customers once per matching order.

interactive.reveal: Conditions on the outer-joined table belong in ON if you want to keep unmatched rows.

title: Normal Forms and Anomalies
objectives: Spot update, insert and delete anomalies
Apply first, second and third normal form
Decide when to denormalise on purpose

cards.title: One fact in one place
cards.body: Normalisation organises tables so each fact is stored once. If a customer’s address is copied onto every order, changing it means updating many rows, and missing one leaves the data contradicting itself.

cards.title: Worked example: splitting a flat orders table
cards.body: A spreadsheet-style table shows all three anomalies at once.
steps: Assume: orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_name, customer_city, product_ids "12,15,19")
Product list in one column breaks 1NF: move it to order_items(order_id, product_id)
customer_name and customer_city depend on customer_id, not on the order: move them to customers
Result tables: customers, orders(order_id, customer_id), order_items(order_id, product_id)
cards.note: Result. Three tables, and each customer’s city is stored once. Renaming a city is one update, a customer can exist before ordering, and deleting their last order does not erase them.

cards.title: Three normal forms in practice
cards.body: Each form removes one kind of misplaced dependency.
steps: 1NF: one value per column, no repeating groups or lists
2NF: with a composite key, every column depends on the whole key
3NF: no column depends on another non-key column
Rule of thumb: every column describes the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key
Higher forms (BCNF, 4NF) handle rarer cases

cards.title: When to denormalise
cards.body: Copying data on purpose can be right for read-heavy paths: an order stores the price at purchase time (which is a different fact from today’s price), or a counter is kept on a post to avoid counting on every view. Each copy needs a clear owner and an update path.

cards.title: Trap: storing lists in a text column
cards.body: A column holding “12,15,19” cannot be indexed, joined or constrained per item, and updating one id means rewriting the string. Use a link table, or the database’s array or JSON type only when you never need to query items individually.

cards.title: Edge case: denormalised counters drift
cards.body: Storing a comment_count on posts saves a COUNT query, but every code path that adds or deletes a comment must update it in the same transaction. A bulk delete, a manual fix or a retried job that skips the update leaves the count wrong with no error. Keep a periodic job that recomputes it from the source rows, or derive it with a trigger or materialised view.

questions.prompt: The customer’s city is stored on every order row. They move. What is this risk called?

choices.label: A deadlock
An update anomaly
A delete anomaly
A phantom read

questions.explanation: One fact in many rows can be updated inconsistently.

questions.prompt: order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name): which normal form does product_name break?

choices.label: None; the table is already fully normalised
First normal form, because it holds a list of names
Second normal form: it depends on product_id alone, part of the key
Third normal form only, because names are non-key data

questions.explanation: A column that depends on part of a composite key violates 2NF.

questions.prompt: An order line stores unit_price even though products has a price. Is that a normalisation mistake?

choices.label: No: denormalised copies are always harmless
No: the price at purchase is a different fact from today’s price
Yes: storing it there breaks first normal form
Yes: a price may only ever live in products

questions.explanation: Historical values are facts in their own right.

questions.prompt: All of a customer’s details live only on their orders. Their last order is deleted. What happens?

choices.label: Nothing; details live in a cache
The customer’s details are lost (a delete anomaly)
The customer row is archived automatically
The foreign key blocks the delete

questions.explanation: Facts about one thing vanish with rows about another.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to normalise a flat table.

items.label: Split lists in a column into a separate table (1NF)
Add foreign keys between the new tables
Move columns that depend on non-key columns (3NF)
Move columns that depend on part of a composite key (2NF)
Check common queries still work with joins

questions.explanation: Each step removes one kind of misplaced dependency.

questions.prompt: A product page shows a review count. Counting reviews on every view is slow at peak.
constraints: The count may lag by a few seconds
Reviews are the source of truth

approaches.label: Fully normalised: count on every page view
Keep a review_count on products, updated when reviews change
Store the full review list on the product row

rationaleOptions.label: Normalised designs are always faster
Embedding all reviews in the product row is simplest
The expensive work moves to the rare write
Reviews stay the source of truth; the counter can be rebuilt

rationaleConflicts.r3: Counting many rows on every read is the slow part here.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It breaks 1NF, bloats the row and makes each review hard to update.

questions.explanation: Denormalise deliberately: one derived value, one owner, rebuildable from the source.

flashcards.back: Store each fact once to avoid anomalies.
Every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

flashcards.front: When is a copied value fine?
flashcards.back: When it is a different fact (price at purchase) or a deliberate, owned cache.

sources.title: E. F. Codd: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (ACM, 1970)
W. Kent: A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory (CACM, 1983)
R. Fagin: Multivalued Dependencies and a New Normal Form for Relational Databases (ACM TODS, 1977)

mechanism.title: Why dependencies decide table boundaries
steps: A functional dependency says one set of columns determines another: customer_id determines customer_name. Normal forms are rules about which dependencies a table may contain, so that each fact is recorded exactly once.
First normal form asks for atomic values: no lists in a column and no repeating groups (phone1, phone2, phone3). Lists become rows in a child table, which can then be indexed and constrained.

Second normal form applies to composite keys. In order_items(order_id, product_id, …), a column such as product_name depends only on product_id, so it belongs in products. Tables with a single-column key are automatically in 2NF if they are in 1NF.

Third normal form removes transitive dependencies: if orders has customer_id and customer_city, the city depends on the customer, not the order. Boyce–Codd normal form tightens this for tables with overlapping candidate keys.

The anomalies normalisation prevents: update anomalies (one change, many rows), insert anomalies (cannot record a customer without an order), and delete anomalies (deleting an order deletes the only record of a customer).

Denormalisation trades these risks for read speed or simplicity: summary columns, copied display names, or document-shaped storage. It is safe when the copy has a single writer, a defined refresh path, and can be rebuilt from the normalised source.

useWhen: Normalise by default for transactional data that many features update.
Denormalise specific read paths once measurement shows a need, with an owner for each copy.
avoidWhen: Avoid lists and repeating groups in columns you need to query.
Avoid copying mutable facts (names, addresses) without a plan to keep them in sync.

rows: Lists and repeating groups in a row
Dependence on part of a composite key

numbers.title: The cost of one copied fact
assumptions: A customer’s name is copied onto each of their orders (illustrative)
200,000 customers, 50 orders each on average; 1% of customers change their name each year
steps: Orders holding names: 200,000 × 50 = 10,000,000 rows.
Name changes per year: 2,000 customers × 50 rows = 100,000 row updates, against 2,000 in a normalised design.
Any update that fails half-way leaves orders showing different names for one customer.
If the name on an order is meant to be the name at purchase time, the copy is correct and should not be updated at all.
numbers.result: Copies multiply write work and inconsistency risk; keep them only when they record a distinct fact or a measured read need.

india.title: Normalisation in Codd’s relational model
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Codd’s 1970 paper introduced normalisation as eliminating nested (non-simple) domains, which is first normal form, and his follow-up work defined the second and third normal forms. The PostgreSQL documentation provides arrays and JSON types for cases where storing a list in one column is a deliberate choice, and constraints and foreign keys for the normalised design.

pitfalls.trap: “Joins are slow, so we put everything in one table.”
pitfalls.say: “That creates update anomalies; I’d normalise first and denormalise a measured hot path with a clear owner.”

pitfalls.trap: “Storing the price on the order line is duplication.”
pitfalls.say: “It is the price at purchase, a different fact; it should not change when the catalogue does.”

takeaways: Store each fact once; anomalies come from copies.
1NF: atomic values. 2NF: whole key. 3NF: nothing but the key.
Historical values are separate facts, not duplicates.
Denormalise deliberately, with an owner and a rebuild path.

interactive.title: Which anomaly?
interactive.prompt: A courses table holds (course_id, teacher_name, teacher_email). A teacher who teaches five courses changes email; only three rows get updated.

choices.label: An update anomaly: two rows now show the old email
choices.feedback: Right: the email depends on the teacher, not the course, so it is stored five times.

choices.label: An insert anomaly
choices.feedback: That would be being unable to add a teacher without a course.

choices.label: A delete anomaly
choices.feedback: That would be losing the teacher when their last course is deleted.

interactive.reveal: Move teacher details to a teachers table referenced by courses. The email is then stored once and updated once.

title: B-tree and Hash Indexes
objectives: Explain how a B-tree finds a row in a few page reads
Order the columns of a composite index
Weigh an index’s read benefit against its write cost

cards.title: A sorted map to the rows
cards.body: An index is a separate structure, kept in sync with the table, that maps column values to row locations. A B-tree keeps values sorted in wide pages, so the database can jump to a value or a range in a few page reads instead of scanning the whole table.

cards.title: Worked example: how deep is the tree?
cards.body: Each B-tree page holds hundreds of keys, so the tree stays shallow.
steps: Assume: 100 million rows, about 500 keys per page (an illustrative fan-out)
Levels ≈ log₅₀₀(100,000,000)
So about 3 levels from root to leaf
cards.note: Result. About three page reads to find any row among 100 million, and the top levels are usually cached in memory. Without the index, the database reads the whole table.

cards.title: Choosing a composite index
cards.body: Column order decides which queries the index can serve.
steps: Index on (customer_id, created_at)
Serves WHERE customer_id = ?
Serves WHERE customer_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at
Cannot efficiently serve WHERE created_at > ? alone
Put equality columns first, then the range or sort column

cards.title: Hash indexes
cards.body: A hash index maps a hash of the value to rows. It supports only equality (=), not ranges or ordering. In PostgreSQL the default B-tree also handles equality well, so hash indexes are a niche choice; other engines use hashing mainly in memory.

cards.title: Trap: an index for every column
cards.body: Every index is updated on every insert, and on updates that touch its columns, and takes disk and memory. Unused indexes slow writes for nothing. Index for the queries you actually run, and drop indexes the statistics show are never used.

cards.title: Edge case: an index the query cannot use
cards.body: A B-tree index on email does not help WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com', because the index stores email values, not lower(email). The same applies to LIKE '%term' (no fixed prefix) and to comparing a text column with a number when the database must convert each row. Index the expression itself, or change the query so it compares the stored column directly.

questions.prompt: Index on (customer_id, created_at). Which query can use it best?

choices.label: WHERE status = ’paid’ ORDER BY total
WHERE total > 100 AND status = ’paid’
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > ’2026-01-01’
WHERE created_at > ’2026-01-01’ alone

questions.explanation: The leading column must be constrained for a normal B-tree lookup.

questions.prompt: Which query can a hash index not help with?

choices.label: WHERE id = 42
WHERE email = ’a@example.com’
WHERE sku = ’AB-1’
WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 20

questions.explanation: Hashes do not preserve order, so ranges need a B-tree.

questions.prompt: A table has 12 indexes and inserts are slow. What is a likely cause?

choices.label: Indexes lock the whole table on insert
Indexes make the table read-only
Every insert must update all 12 indexes
The planner scans every index per insert

questions.explanation: Write cost grows with the number of indexes.

questions.prompt: Why do B-trees stay only 3–4 levels deep for very large tables?

choices.label: They keep the whole table in memory
Each page holds hundreds of keys, so the fan-out is large
They rebuild the tree into one level nightly
They store only a sample of the rows

questions.explanation: Depth grows with the logarithm to a large base.

questions.prompt: Order a B-tree lookup for one key.

items.label: Fetch the row from the table (unless the index covers the query)
Read the root page
Find the key in the leaf
Follow the next pointer down to a leaf page
Follow the pointer for the key’s range to an inner page

questions.explanation: Root to leaf, then the table row.

assumptions: Fan-out 1,000
Full pages
questions.explanation: Sanity check: going from a million to a billion rows adds only one level, which is why indexed lookups stay fast as tables grow.

flashcards.back: Equality, ranges and ordering.
Equality only.
Equality columns first, then range or sort columns.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes

mechanism.title: How indexes are structured and used
steps: A B-tree is a balanced tree of fixed-size pages. Inner pages hold separator keys and child pointers; leaf pages hold keys in order with pointers to table rows, and are linked to their neighbours so range scans walk along the leaves.

Lookups cost one page read per level. Because fan-out is in the hundreds, depth grows very slowly: each extra level multiplies capacity by the fan-out. The root and upper levels are hot and usually stay in memory.

A composite index sorts by its first column, then the second within equal first values, and so on, like a phone book by surname then first name. It serves conditions on a leading prefix of its columns; equality on early columns and a range or ORDER BY on the next is the ideal shape.

If an index contains every column a query needs, the database can answer from the index alone (an index-only scan in PostgreSQL, which also checks a visibility map). INCLUDE columns add payload to leaves without making them part of the key.

Hash indexes store hash values and support only equality. B-trees also support uniqueness, ranges, sorting and prefix matches such as LIKE ’abc%’ (with suitable collation or operator class), which is why they are the default.

Each index adds write work, storage and memory pressure, and must be maintained during bulk loads. The planner may also ignore an index when a query returns a large fraction of the table, because reading the table sequentially is cheaper.

useWhen: Index columns used in selective WHERE conditions, joins and ORDER BY with LIMIT.
Design composite indexes around your most frequent query shapes.
avoidWhen: Avoid indexes on columns with very few distinct values when queries return most rows.
Avoid duplicate or overlapping indexes; (a) is redundant next to (a, b) for most uses.

rows: Equality + range on known query shapes

numbers.title: Read benefit vs write cost of one index
assumptions: Table of 50 million rows; a query by customer_id runs 2,000 times a second (illustrative)
Inserts: 500 a second; an index adds about 3 page writes per insert (illustrative)
steps: Without the index each query scans 50 million rows; at 2,000 queries a second that is 100 billion rows a second, far beyond one server.
With it, each query reads about 3–4 index pages plus the matching rows.
Write cost: 500 × 3 = 1,500 extra page writes a second, spread across cached pages and the write-ahead log.
Here the index is essential; an index serving a query that runs once a day would rarely justify the same write cost.
numbers.result: Weigh how often each index is read against how often the table is written.

Composite indexes serve leading-column conditions; put equality first.

title: How the Query Planner Works
objectives: Explain why SQL needs a planner
Read the main nodes of a query plan
Use estimates vs actual rows to find a bad plan

cards.title: You say what, it decides how
cards.body: SQL describes the result, not the steps. The planner considers ways to produce it (which index, which join order, which join algorithm), estimates each one’s cost from table statistics, and runs the cheapest. Good statistics are what make its guesses good.

cards.title: Worked example: when the planner skips your index
cards.body: Selectivity decides between an index scan and a full scan.
steps: Assume: 10 million rows in about 100,000 pages
Query A matches 0.01%: about 1,000 rows, so at most about 1,000 page reads by index (far fewer if matching rows sit together on disk)
Query B matches 30%: about 3 million rows, spread over nearly every page
Reading every page in order (sequential scan) beats 3 million random index lookups
cards.note: Result. The planner uses the index for query A and a sequential scan for query B. Ignoring an index for an unselective filter is usually the right call, not a bug.

cards.title: Reading a plan
cards.body: Plans are trees; data flows from the leaves up.
steps: Leaves are scans: sequential scan, index scan, bitmap scan
Inner nodes join or combine: nested loop, hash join, merge join
Above them: sort, aggregate, limit
Each node shows estimated cost and rows; with ANALYZE, actual time and rows too
Look for the node where estimated and actual rows differ most

cards.title: Three join algorithms
cards.body: A nested loop looks up matching rows for each outer row, which is ideal when the outer side is small and the inner side is indexed. A hash join builds a hash table of the smaller input and probes it, good for large unsorted inputs. A merge join walks two inputs already sorted on the join key.

cards.title: Trap: running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write
cards.body: EXPLAIN only plans; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement to measure it. On an UPDATE or DELETE that changes data. Wrap it in a transaction you roll back, or test on a copy.

cards.title: Edge case: stale statistics
cards.body: The planner estimates row counts from sampled statistics. After a large bulk load or delete, those statistics can be far off, so it picks a nested-loop join for what is now millions of rows and a fast query becomes slow overnight. Run ANALYZE (or the database’s equivalent) after big data changes, and compare estimated with actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

questions.prompt: A filter matches 40% of a large table. The planner chose a sequential scan despite an index. Why?

choices.label: Planners ignore every index on very large tables
Sequential scans always win for any filter at all
Reading the table in order is cheaper than millions of random lookups
The index must be corrupted and needs rebuilding

questions.explanation: Low selectivity makes index lookups more expensive than a scan.

questions.prompt: Joining 20 rows to a 50-million-row table on an indexed column. Which join is likely?

choices.label: Hash join over the whole large table
Nested loop with index lookups
Cross join filtered afterwards
Merge join after sorting both inputs

questions.explanation: Twenty index probes are far cheaper than reading 50 million rows.

questions.prompt: A plan estimates 10 rows for a node that actually returns 2 million. What is the likely root cause?

choices.label: The server has too little memory
Stale or insufficient statistics
Too many indexes on the table
The query uses a LEFT JOIN

questions.explanation: Misestimates lead to wrong join and scan choices; refresh statistics first.

questions.prompt: What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE add over EXPLAIN?

choices.label: It runs the query and reports actual rows and time
It shows the plan without running it
It suggests indexes to create
It rewrites the query to be faster

questions.explanation: Actual numbers reveal misestimates, at the cost of executing.

questions.prompt: Order how a database handles a query.

items.label: Plan: estimate costs and choose a plan
Parse the SQL text
Rewrite (expand views, apply rules)
Return rows to the client
Execute the plan

questions.explanation: Planning sits between understanding the query and running it.

questions.prompt: A table has 10 million rows and a filter keeps 0.2% of them. About how many rows does the planner expect?
assumptions: Uniform distribution assumed
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 20,000 rows is selective enough that an index is likely to win; at 20% it would be 2 million rows and a sequential scan would probably be chosen.

flashcards.back: Estimated cost, using table statistics.
The outer side is small and the inner side is indexed.
Plan only vs plan plus actual execution.

mechanism.title: How plans are chosen and how to check them
steps: After parsing, the planner enumerates candidate plans: scan methods for each table, join orders, and join algorithms. For many-table joins the number of orders explodes, so planners use heuristics or genetic search beyond a threshold.

Each plan gets an estimated cost from a model of page reads (sequential cheaper than random) and CPU work per row. The inputs are statistics: row counts, distinct values, most common values and histograms per column, gathered by ANALYZE (and autovacuum in PostgreSQL).

Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition keeps. The planner multiplies selectivities of separate conditions as if they were independent, which goes wrong for correlated columns such as city and postcode; extended statistics can fix that.

Scans: a sequential scan reads all pages in order; an index scan follows the index and fetches rows; a bitmap scan collects matching row locations from one or more indexes, sorts them by page and reads each page once, a middle ground for medium selectivity.

Joins: nested loop (cheap with a small outer input and an indexed inner), hash join (builds a hash table from the smaller input, needs memory), merge join (needs both inputs sorted). Sorts and hashes that exceed working memory spill to disk, which plans show.

Diagnosing: run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a representative query, find the node where actual rows differ from the estimate by orders of magnitude, then fix the cause: refresh statistics, add an index, rewrite a condition so it can use an index, or adjust memory settings.

useWhen: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE on slow queries with production-like data volumes.
Keep statistics fresh after bulk loads and large deletes.
avoidWhen: Avoid forcing plans with hints as a first resort; fix statistics and indexes first.
Avoid testing plans on tiny development tables; plans change with data size.

rows: Many random reads if estimates are wrong
Lossy pages on very large results
Spilling to disk when memory is short
Disaster when the outer estimate is far too low

numbers.title: How one misestimate turns into a slow plan
assumptions: The planner expects 10 rows from a filter; actually 200,000 match (illustrative)
It chooses a nested loop with an index lookup per outer row, each costing about 0.05 ms
steps: Expected work: 10 lookups × 0.05 ms = 0.5 ms.
A hash join over the same inputs might take a few hundred milliseconds.
Refreshing statistics so the estimate is close lets the planner pick the hash join itself.
numbers.result: Plans fail through bad estimates far more often than through a bad cost model; compare estimated with actual rows first.

The “Statistics Used by the Planner” chapter explains the per-column statistics and extended statistics for correlated columns.

Selective filters use indexes; unselective ones scan.

title: Transactions in Practice
objectives: Group writes so they succeed or fail together
Keep transactions short and know what they hold
Use savepoints and retries correctly

cards.title: All or nothing
cards.body: A transaction groups statements so they commit together or not at all. Moving money means debiting one account and crediting another; if the process crashes between the two, the transaction is rolled back and neither change is visible.

cards.title: Misconception: each statement is safe on its own
cards.body: Without an explicit transaction most databases run each statement in its own transaction (autocommit). Two separate UPDATEs can therefore leave the data half-changed if the second fails or the app crashes between them. Multi-step changes need BEGIN … COMMIT around them.

cards.title: A money transfer, step by step
cards.body: The checks and both writes sit in one transaction.
steps: BEGIN
Read the source balance with a lock (or rely on a check constraint balance >= 0)
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance − 100 WHERE id = A
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = B
INSERT the transfer record, then COMMIT; any error before this means ROLLBACK

cards.title: What ACID promises
cards.body: Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other’s partial work (to the degree the isolation level says). Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash.

cards.title: Trap: calling other services inside a transaction
cards.body: A transaction that waits on an external HTTP call holds its locks and its connection for the whole wait. If the call takes seconds, other writers queue behind it. Do external calls before or after the transaction, and record the intent in the database (an outbox table) if both must happen.

cards.title: Edge case: the commit succeeded but the reply was lost
cards.body: If the connection drops while COMMIT is in flight, the client cannot tell whether the transaction committed. Blindly retrying can apply it twice. Give the write an idempotency key or a unique business identifier so a retry is detected, or check for the row before trying again.

choices.label: The database retries the second one
Neither ran, because the batch failed
The first update is committed; the second is not
Both are rolled back automatically

questions.prompt: Which ACID property means a committed change survives a power cut?

choices.label: Durability
Consistency
Atomicity

choices.label: The lock and connection are held for those 4 seconds
The payment provider sees uncommitted data
The transaction cannot be rolled back
Durability is lost for the order

questions.prompt: What does a savepoint let you do?

choices.label: Roll back part of a transaction and continue
Share a transaction between connections
Skip the write-ahead log
Commit half of a transaction early

items.label: Debit A, credit B and insert the transfer record
Read A’s balance with SELECT … FOR UPDATE
COMMIT

constraints: The provider call can take seconds
A charge without an order is unacceptable

approaches.label: Reserve stock in a short transaction, call the provider outside it, then confirm or release in a second short transaction
One transaction that wraps the provider call

A single long transaction guarantees the charge is rolled back too

flashcards.back: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability.
Each statement is its own transaction unless you BEGIN one.
A marker you can roll back to without abandoning the whole transaction.

mechanism.title: How transactions behave and what they cost
steps: BEGIN starts a transaction; COMMIT makes all its changes visible and durable at once; ROLLBACK discards them. If the connection drops or the server crashes before COMMIT, the database rolls the transaction back during recovery.

In PostgreSQL an error inside a transaction aborts it: every later statement fails until you ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint). Savepoints let you try a step, and undo just that step on failure, without losing earlier work.

Consistency in ACID means the database’s rules hold: constraints, foreign keys and triggers are checked, and a transaction that would break them fails. It does not mean application-level correctness unless those rules are written as constraints.

While a transaction runs it holds row locks on what it wrote, keeps a snapshot that prevents cleanup of old row versions, and occupies a connection. Long or idle-in-transaction sessions therefore cause lock waits, table bloat and connection exhaustion.

Under stricter isolation levels a transaction can fail with a serialisation error because of a concurrent one. The correct response is to retry the whole transaction from the start, so transaction code should be safe to re-run.

Transactions stop at the database boundary. Work involving other systems (payments, emails, queues) uses patterns such as the transactional outbox: write the business change and an outbox row in one transaction, and let a separate process deliver the message.

useWhen: Wrap every multi-statement change that must be all-or-nothing in one transaction.
Keep transactions short: do slow reads, computation and network calls outside.
avoidWhen: Avoid holding a transaction open while waiting for a user or an external service.
Avoid retrying only the failed statement after a serialisation error; retry the whole transaction.

rows: Changes plus messages to other systems

numbers.title: How a slow step inside a transaction limits throughput
assumptions: Every order updates one hot row (a stock counter for a popular item) inside its transaction (illustrative)
The row lock is held until commit
steps: If the transaction takes 5 ms, at most 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 orders a second can update that row.
If it includes a 300 ms external call, the limit drops to about 3 a second, and the rest queue.
Moving the call outside brings it back to about 200 a second.
Splitting the counter into several rows, or reserving stock in batches, raises the ceiling further.
numbers.result: Time inside a transaction is time a lock is held; shortening transactions raises the throughput of hot rows directly.

It notes that without BEGIN each statement is treated as its own transaction, and the reliability chapter explains how the write-ahead log makes committed transactions durable.

Without BEGIN, each statement commits on its own.

title: Isolation Levels and Their Anomalies
objectives: Name the read anomalies and the lost update and write skew problems
Match each isolation level to the anomalies it prevents
Handle serialisation failures with retries

cards.title: What concurrent transactions can see
cards.body: Isolation decides how much one transaction can observe of others running at the same time. Stronger isolation removes more surprising results but blocks or aborts more transactions. Most databases do not default to the strongest level.

cards.title: Worked example: the lost update
cards.body: Read, compute, write in two transactions at once loses one change.
steps: Assume: stock = 10; two orders each buy 1, at Read Committed
T1 reads 10; T2 reads 10
T1 writes 9 and commits; T2 writes 9 and commits
Stock shows 9 though 2 items were sold
cards.note: Result. One sale vanished. Fixes: an atomic UPDATE stock = stock − 1, a SELECT … FOR UPDATE lock, a version check in the WHERE clause, or a stricter isolation level that aborts T2.

cards.title: The read anomalies
cards.body: Each is a different way to see data change under you.
steps: Dirty read: seeing another transaction’s uncommitted change
Non-repeatable read: the same row read twice gives different values
Phantom: the same query returns new rows the second time
Write skew: two transactions each check a rule, then write different rows, breaking it together
Serializable isolation prevents all of these

cards.title: Levels in PostgreSQL
cards.body: PostgreSQL offers Read Committed (the default; each statement sees data committed before it began), Repeatable Read (one snapshot for the whole transaction, which also prevents phantoms in PostgreSQL) and Serializable (adds detection of dangerous patterns such as write skew and aborts one transaction). Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed.

cards.title: Trap: not retrying serialisation failures
cards.body: At Repeatable Read and Serializable, PostgreSQL aborts a transaction that conflicts with a concurrent one, with SQLSTATE 40001. That is expected behaviour, not a bug. Code must catch it and re-run the whole transaction, or users see random errors under load.

cards.title: Same name, different behaviour: MySQL InnoDB
cards.body: InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read. Plain SELECTs see a snapshot, but UPDATE and DELETE act on the latest committed row, so read-then-write code can still lose an update. Use an atomic UPDATE or SELECT … FOR UPDATE. On a range scan that takes next-key locks (a row and the gap before it); a lookup by a unique key locks just the row.

mechanism.title: What each level guarantees and how it is implemented
steps: The SQL standard defines four levels by the phenomena they forbid: Read Uncommitted (allows dirty reads), Read Committed (no dirty reads), Repeatable Read (no non-repeatable reads) and Serializable (results equal to some serial order). Databases may give stronger guarantees than the minimum.

At Read Committed in PostgreSQL each statement takes a new snapshot. Two statements in one transaction can therefore see different data, and read-then-write logic in application code is exposed to lost updates.

At Repeatable Read PostgreSQL uses one snapshot for the whole transaction (snapshot isolation). If it tries to update a row that a concurrent transaction changed after the snapshot, it is aborted with a serialisation failure instead of overwriting, which prevents lost updates.

Snapshot isolation still allows write skew, because the two transactions write different rows. Serializable in PostgreSQL uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation: it tracks read/write dependencies and aborts one transaction when a cycle could make the result non-serial.

The same level names behave differently across products. MySQL’s InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read, and its plain SELECTs read one snapshot taken at the first read. Its documentation notes that this snapshot applies to SELECTs, not necessarily to UPDATE and DELETE: those act on the latest committed rows. So an InnoDB read-then-write at Repeatable Read can still lose an update where PostgreSQL would raise a serialisation failure. Locking reads (SELECT … FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE) and range updates in InnoDB take next-key locks (a row plus the gap before it) to block phantom inserts, and InnoDB’s Serializable turns plain SELECTs into SELECT … FOR SHARE when autocommit is off, so it is lock-based rather than SSI. SQL Server defaults to lock-based Read Committed, with an optional row-versioning mode (READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT) and a separate SNAPSHOT level. Oracle offers Read Committed (default) and a Serializable level that is snapshot-based. Check the level in your database’s documentation rather than assuming the name tells you the behaviour.

Alternatives to raising the level for one operation: atomic single-statement updates, SELECT … FOR UPDATE to lock the rows you will change, optimistic version columns checked in the UPDATE, or constraints that make the bad state impossible.

useWhen: Use Read Committed with atomic updates or row locks for simple read-modify-write cases.
Use Serializable for rules that span several rows, with automatic retries.
avoidWhen: Avoid assuming the default level prevents lost updates in read-then-write code.
Avoid relying on level names meaning the same in every database product (InnoDB’s Repeatable Read does not abort a stale UPDATE the way PostgreSQL’s does).

rows: For contrast: InnoDB Repeatable Read (MySQL default)
Plain SELECTs see the snapshot; locking reads use next-key locks
Possible; stale UPDATEs are not aborted

numbers.title: How retries scale with contention
assumptions: Serializable transactions; 2% of them abort with serialisation failures at normal load (illustrative)
Each retry has the same chance of conflicting
steps: Expected attempts per transaction: 1 ÷ (1 − 0.02) ≈ 1.02, about 2% extra work.
At peak, conflicts rise to 20%: 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25 attempts, 25% extra work.
Retries add load exactly when contention is highest, so cap them (for example 3–5 attempts) with a short random backoff.
If one hot row causes most conflicts, redesigning that row (splitting counters, queueing updates) beats more retries.
numbers.result: Serializable is affordable at low contention; at high contention, fix the hot spot rather than retrying harder.

india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL “Transaction Isolation” chapter has a table of which phenomena each level allows, notes that Read Uncommitted is treated as Read Committed and that Repeatable Read also prevents phantoms in PostgreSQL. It describes serialisation failures (SQLSTATE 40001) and states that applications using these levels must be prepared to retry transactions.

pitfalls.trap: “We use transactions, so concurrent updates are safe.”

pitfalls.trap: “Serializable errors mean the database is overloaded.”
pitfalls.say: “They are expected conflicts; the fix is to retry the transaction, and reduce hot spots if they are frequent.”

Read Committed allows lost updates in read-then-write code.
Snapshot isolation stops lost updates but allows write skew.
Serializable prevents all anomalies; retry on 40001.

title: Locks and MVCC
objectives: Explain how MVCC lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other
Use row locks deliberately
Prevent and recognise deadlocks

cards.title: Many versions instead of waiting
cards.body: With multi-version concurrency control (MVCC), an update writes a new version of the row instead of changing it in place. Each transaction reads the versions that were committed as of its snapshot, so readers never wait for writers and writers never wait for readers. Writers of the same row still queue behind each other.

cards.title: Worked example: a deadlock between two transfers
cards.body: Opposite lock orders on the same two rows wait for each other forever.
steps: Assume: T1 transfers A → B; T2 transfers B → A, at the same moment
T1 locks row A; T2 locks row B
T1 waits for B; T2 waits for A
The database detects the cycle and aborts one of them
cards.note: Result. One transfer fails with a deadlock error and must be retried. Locking rows in a consistent order (for example, lower account id first) prevents the cycle entirely.

cards.title: Locking rows you are about to change
cards.body: SELECT … FOR UPDATE reads and locks in one step.
steps: BEGIN
SELECT * FROM seats WHERE id = 12 FOR UPDATE: lock the row
Check the seat is free
UPDATE seats SET holder = 7 WHERE id = 12
COMMIT releases the lock; a concurrent booking waited and now sees the seat taken

cards.title: Cleaning up old versions
cards.body: Old row versions stay until no running transaction could need them. In PostgreSQL, VACUUM (usually run automatically) reclaims them. A transaction left open for hours prevents cleanup across the whole database, so tables grow and queries slow down.

cards.title: Trap: schema changes that wait for a strong lock
cards.body: Some ALTER TABLE forms need an exclusive lock. If a long query is running, the ALTER waits, and every new query on the table queues behind the ALTER. A two-second wait can become an outage. Set a short lock timeout and retry.

cards.title: Edge case: long transactions block cleanup
cards.body: MVCC keeps old row versions while any open transaction might still need them. One transaction left open for hours, such as an idle session in a forgotten console, stops PostgreSQL’s VACUUM from removing dead rows, so tables and indexes bloat and queries slow down. Set an idle-in-transaction timeout and alert on old open transactions.

questions.prompt: Under MVCC, a long report is reading a table while another transaction updates rows. What happens?

choices.label: The report sees a mix of old and new values mid-row
The updates block the report until they commit
The report blocks the updates until it finishes
Both proceed; the report reads the versions from its snapshot

questions.explanation: Readers and writers do not block each other under MVCC.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent the A↔B transfer deadlock?

choices.label: Use a much longer lock timeout for transfers
Lock both rows only after updating them
Run all the transfers at Read Uncommitted
Always lock the two accounts in the same order (for example by id)

questions.explanation: Consistent ordering makes a waiting cycle impossible.

questions.prompt: What does SELECT … FOR UPDATE do?

choices.label: Locks the whole table for writes
Locks the selected rows until the transaction ends
Updates the rows immediately
Creates a snapshot for later reads

questions.explanation: Other writers and FOR UPDATE readers of those rows wait.

questions.prompt: A session has been idle in an open transaction for 6 hours. What can this cause in PostgreSQL?

choices.label: Old row versions cannot be cleaned up, so tables bloat
The transaction log is deleted to save space
All writes to the whole database stop at once
Every index is rebuilt automatically overnight

questions.explanation: Its snapshot keeps dead versions alive for everyone.

Kill all sessions, then run the ALTER

Killing sessions is the standard approach

rationaleConflicts.r4: It drops users’ work and is unnecessary if the lock wait is time-boxed.

questions.explanation: Lock queues are first come, first served: a waiting strong lock blocks everyone behind it, so time-box it.

flashcards.back: Writers create new row versions; readers see the versions in their snapshot.
Lock resources in a consistent order.

flashcards.front: Why are long transactions harmful under MVCC?
flashcards.back: They stop old versions being cleaned up.

mechanism.title: How versions and locks coordinate concurrent work
steps: In PostgreSQL each row version records the transaction that created it and the one that deleted or replaced it. A snapshot lists which transactions had committed when it was taken; a version is visible if its creator is in that list and its deleter is not.

Updates create a new version and mark the old one as replaced. Readers using older snapshots still see the old version. Two writers updating the same row do conflict: the second waits for the first to commit or roll back, then either proceeds (Read Committed) or fails (stricter levels).

Explicit row locks: FOR UPDATE (exclusive, for rows you will change), FOR SHARE (stops others changing them), and weaker variants. NOWAIT fails immediately instead of waiting, and SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows, which is how many job queues built on tables hand out work.

Table-level locks are taken by every statement in a mode that matches what it does; ordinary reads and writes take weak modes that do not conflict with each other. DDL such as many ALTER TABLE forms takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which conflicts with everything, including plain reads.

A deadlock is a cycle of waits. PostgreSQL checks for cycles after a short wait (deadlock_timeout, 1 second by default), aborts one transaction, and lets the others continue. Applications should retry the aborted one and fix the lock ordering.

VACUUM removes versions no snapshot can see and updates the visibility map used by index-only scans. Autovacuum runs it in the background; long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions hold back the oldest snapshot and stop it from cleaning up.

useWhen: Use SELECT … FOR UPDATE (or atomic UPDATE statements) for read-check-write on contended rows.
Use SKIP LOCKED for worker queues that pull jobs from a table.
avoidWhen: Avoid leaving transactions open while idle; set an idle-in-transaction timeout.
Avoid running DDL on busy tables without a lock timeout.

rows: Many schema changes; keep very short

numbers.title: How long a blocked schema change can stall a table
assumptions: A report query has been running for 90 s and will run 30 s more (illustrative)
An ALTER TABLE needing ACCESS EXCLUSIVE is started; the table serves 500 queries a second
steps: The ALTER waits 30 s for the report to finish.
Every new query on the table queues behind the ALTER: 500 × 30 = 15,000 queries waiting.
Connection pools fill and the application starts timing out, though the ALTER itself would take milliseconds.
With lock_timeout = 2 s, the ALTER gives up after 2 s (about 1,000 queued queries, which then run) and can retry later.
numbers.result: A lock wait at the head of the queue blocks everything behind it; time-boxing the wait turns an outage into a retry.

india.title: Locking and MVCC in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL concurrency-control chapter states the core MVCC property that reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading. The explicit-locking chapter lists every table lock mode and which ones conflict, describes row-level locks including NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED, and explains deadlock detection and the advice to acquire locks in a consistent order.

pitfalls.trap: “The report is blocking our writes.”
pitfalls.say: “Under MVCC plain reads don’t block writes; I’d look for an open transaction, explicit locks or a waiting DDL statement.”

pitfalls.trap: “Deadlocks mean the database is broken.”
pitfalls.say: “They are cycles in our lock order; I’d lock rows in a consistent order and retry the victim.”

takeaways: MVCC: readers see snapshots and do not block writers.
Writers of the same row still wait for each other.
Lock rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks.
Time-box strong locks; vacuum needs short transactions.

interactive.title: Who waits?
interactive.prompt: T1 runs a long SELECT on a table. T2 updates rows in it. T3 then starts an ALTER TABLE that needs an exclusive lock. T4 runs a simple SELECT afterwards.

choices.label: T3 waits for T1, and T4 waits behind T3
choices.feedback: Right: the ALTER queues for its exclusive lock, and new queries queue behind it.

choices.label: T2 waits for T1
choices.feedback: Under MVCC, the update does not wait for the read.

choices.label: Nobody waits; MVCC prevents all blocking

title: Write-Ahead Logging and Durability
objectives: Explain the write-ahead rule and why commit means “logged”
Describe crash recovery and checkpoints
Weigh durability settings against commit throughput

cards.title: Log first, data later
cards.body: A database does not rewrite table pages on disk at every commit. It appends a description of each change to a sequential log, the write-ahead log (WAL), and makes sure the log reaches durable storage before COMMIT returns. Data pages are written later, in the background.

cards.title: Worked example: commits per second on one stream
cards.body: Each durable commit waits for a flush to stable storage.
steps: Assume: a flush takes 2 ms on this storage (an illustrative figure)
One client committing one row per transaction, one after another: at most 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 commits a second
Batching 50 rows per transaction: still 500 commits, but 25,000 rows a second
Many concurrent clients: the database flushes several commits together (group commit)
cards.note: Result. A single client is capped near 500 commits a second here, set by flush latency rather than CPU. Batching rows or running clients in parallel raises throughput; turning off the flush trades away durability.

cards.title: Recovery after a crash
cards.body: The log is the source of truth for anything not yet on the data files.
steps: Find the last checkpoint recorded in the log
Replay WAL records from that point forward
Changes of committed transactions are restored
Transactions that never committed have no effect
Open the database for connections

cards.title: Checkpoints
cards.body: A checkpoint flushes all changed data pages and records how far the log has been applied. Recovery only replays from the last checkpoint, so more frequent checkpoints mean faster recovery but more write work during normal running.

cards.title: Trap: assuming every layer honours a flush
cards.body: Durability depends on the disk and controller actually persisting data when asked. Volatile write caches without battery or capacitor backing can acknowledge a flush and then lose it on power loss. Use storage that guarantees flushes, or the database cannot keep its promise.

cards.title: Edge case: the disk says written but is not
cards.body: Durability depends on fsync reaching stable storage. Some consumer drives and misconfigured RAID controllers acknowledge a flush while data is still in a volatile cache, so a power cut loses commits the database reported as durable. Use drives with power-loss protection or a battery-backed cache, and test with a tool that pulls power, not just a clean shutdown.

questions.prompt: When COMMIT returns with default durable settings, what is guaranteed to be on stable storage?

choices.label: Every updated index page
The WAL records for the transaction
A full backup of the table
Every changed table page

questions.explanation: Pages can be rebuilt from the log; the log must be flushed.

questions.prompt: Why does a database write to a sequential log instead of updating pages at commit?

choices.label: Table pages are read-only once they are created
Appending to one log is faster than many random page writes
Log files never need to be flushed to disk
The log removes the need for any indexes at all

questions.explanation: Sequential appends are cheap; pages are written in the background.

questions.prompt: With asynchronous commit enabled, what can happen after a crash?

choices.label: Uncommitted transactions become committed
Every transaction since startup is lost
The database may be corrupted
The last few reported-as-committed transactions may be lost

questions.explanation: It risks recent commits, not consistency.

questions.prompt: Checkpoints happen less often. What changes?

choices.label: Less background writing, but longer recovery after a crash
Commits stop being durable until the next checkpoint
Faster recovery and also less background writing
The write-ahead log becomes unnecessary

questions.explanation: Recovery replays everything since the last checkpoint.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when a transaction commits.

items.label: Change pages in memory
Write the changed pages to data files later
Report COMMIT success to the client
Flush the WAL to stable storage
Append WAL records describing the changes

questions.explanation: The log reaches disk before the client hears “committed”.

questions.prompt: A flush takes 4 ms. One client commits one transaction at a time. About how many commits per second can it reach?
assumptions: One flush per commit
No batching
questions.explanation: Design implication: if one stream must do more, batch several rows per transaction or run commits concurrently so group commit shares each flush.

flashcards.back: Log records reach stable storage before the data pages they describe.
WAL from the last checkpoint.
Losing the most recent commits, not corruption.

mechanism.title: How the log makes commits durable
steps: Changes are made to pages in a memory buffer. Before a changed page may be written to the data files, the WAL records describing that change must be on stable storage: the write-ahead rule. This means any page on disk can be brought up to date, or corrected, from the log.

At commit, the database appends a commit record and flushes the log up to it. Because the log is written sequentially, one flush covers everything before it, which lets concurrent commits share a single flush (group commit).

Crash recovery reads the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies the changes. In PostgreSQL, visibility rules then ensure transactions without a commit record have no effect. Other databases also run an undo phase for uncommitted changes.

Checkpoints write all dirty pages and record a position in the log; older log segments can then be recycled or archived. To guard against torn pages (a page half-written during a crash), PostgreSQL logs a full image of each page the first time it changes after a checkpoint.
The same log feeds replication and point-in-time recovery: streaming WAL to standbys keeps them in sync, and archiving WAL segments with a base backup lets you restore to any moment.

Settings trade safety for speed. PostgreSQL’s synchronous_commit = off returns before the flush, risking a short window of recent commits (bounded by a few times the WAL writer delay) but never corruption. Turning off fsync entirely risks corruption and is only for disposable data.

useWhen: Keep durable commits for data you cannot recreate; batch writes to raise throughput.
Use asynchronous commit for data where losing the last fraction of a second is acceptable, such as some logs or metrics.
avoidWhen: Avoid disabling fsync on any database you care about.
Avoid storage whose write cache can lose acknowledged flushes on power failure.

rows: Nothing even if the primary dies
Data that must survive losing a server

numbers.title: Group commit at work
assumptions: Flush time 2 ms (illustrative); 40 clients committing concurrently
Each flush can include every commit record written before it started
steps: Without sharing, 40 clients would need 40 flushes per round: 80 ms of flushing.
With group commit, commits arriving during a flush ride on the next one; roughly one flush serves many of them.
If each flush carries 20 commits on average, throughput is 20 × 500 = 10,000 commits a second instead of 500.
This is why total commit throughput rises with concurrency even though each commit still waits about one flush.
numbers.result: Flush latency limits each client, not the server; concurrency and batching spread one flush over many commits.

india.title: WAL in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL WAL chapter explains the central idea that changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed, and that this lets the server avoid flushing data pages at every commit. The reliability chapter warns about disk write caches that do not survive power loss, and the asynchronous-commit chapter describes exactly what is risked when commits do not wait for the flush.

pitfalls.trap: “COMMIT means the table file on disk is updated.”
pitfalls.say: “It means the log is flushed; pages are written later and can be rebuilt from the log.”

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll turn off fsync to speed up inserts.”
pitfalls.say: “That risks corruption; I’d batch inserts or use asynchronous commit for low-value data.”

takeaways: WAL records reach stable storage before data pages and before COMMIT returns.
Recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint.
Flush latency caps commits per stream; batching and group commit raise throughput.
Asynchronous commit risks recent commits; fsync off risks corruption.

interactive.title: What survives the crash?
interactive.prompt: A server runs with synchronous_commit = off. Transaction X commits, the client hears “success”, and 50 ms later the server loses power.

choices.label: X may be lost, but the database is consistent
choices.feedback: Right: the commit returned before its WAL flush, so a short window of commits can disappear without corrupting anything.

choices.label: X is guaranteed to survive
choices.feedback: That is the default setting, which waits for the flush.

choices.label: The database is corrupted and must be restored
choices.feedback: Asynchronous commit only risks recent commits; data integrity is kept.

interactive.reveal: Asynchronous commit trades a small, bounded loss window for faster commits. Use it only where losing the last moment of writes is acceptable.

title: Database Replication Basics
objectives: Compare physical and logical replication
Explain synchronous vs asynchronous replication and lag
Handle reads from replicas correctly

cards.title: Copies kept up to date
cards.body: Replication keeps one or more standby databases in step with a primary by shipping the primary’s changes to them. Standbys can take over if the primary fails and can serve read-only queries, but in the common asynchronous setup they are slightly behind.

cards.title: Worked example: what an asynchronous failover can lose
cards.body: Replication lag turns into lost writes if the primary dies.
steps: Assume: asynchronous replication with 2 s of lag at peak (illustrative)
The primary commits 300 transactions a second
It fails and the standby is promoted
Commits in the last 2 s never reached the standby: up to 300 × 2 = 600 transactions
cards.note: Result. Up to about 600 acknowledged transactions are missing after failover under these assumptions. Synchronous replication to at least one standby closes that window, at the cost of a network round trip on every commit.

cards.title: Read your own write from a replica
cards.body: A user saves a profile and the next page reads from a lagging replica.
steps: User updates their name on the primary
The next request reads from a replica 500 ms behind
The page shows the old name, as if the save failed
Fix: read from the primary for a short time after that user writes
Or wait until the replica has replayed past the write’s log position

cards.title: Physical vs logical
cards.body: Physical (streaming) replication ships the write-ahead log, producing an exact byte-level copy of the whole cluster, same major version. Logical replication sends row changes for chosen tables, so subscribers can be a different version or have other tables and indexes, which suits upgrades and selective copies.

cards.title: Trap: treating a replica as a backup
cards.body: A replica copies every change, including mistakes: a dropped table or a bad UPDATE reaches the standby within seconds. Backups with point-in-time recovery (a base backup plus archived WAL) let you restore to the moment before the mistake.

cards.title: Failure story: one command on the wrong server
cards.body: Publicly reported by GitLab in its January 2017 post-mortem: while fixing replication lag, an engineer deleted the data directory on the primary database instead of the replica. Several backup methods turned out not to be working, and about six hours of database changes were lost. The lesson they drew: a replica is not a backup, and a backup is only real once a restore has been tested.

questions.prompt: What does synchronous replication add to each commit?

choices.label: A second write-ahead log on the primary
A full copy of the table to the standby

choices.label: Synchronous physical replication

Restoring last night’s backup

choices.label: A read replica
