mechanism.title: How changes reach standbys
steps: Physical streaming replication sends WAL records from the primary to standbys as they are written. Standbys replay them continuously and can serve read-only queries (hot standby). They are byte-for-byte copies, so they must run the same major version and contain every database in the cluster.

Logical replication decodes the WAL into row-level changes for published tables and applies them on subscribers. Subscribers are ordinary writable databases, can have different indexes and versions, and can receive only some tables, but schema changes and sequences need extra handling.

Asynchronous replication returns from COMMIT once the primary has flushed locally. Lag is usually small but grows under heavy writes, long-running queries on the standby, or network trouble. Synchronous replication waits for one or more standbys to confirm, adding at least one network round trip per commit.

Failover promotes a standby to primary. The hard part is making sure the old primary stops accepting writes (fencing); otherwise two primaries accept conflicting writes (split brain). Most teams use a tested failover manager rather than manual steps.

Reads from replicas need a consistency plan: route a user’s reads to the primary briefly after they write, wait for the replica to pass the write’s log position, or accept stale reads where they are harmless (public listings, analytics).
Backups are separate: a base backup plus continuously archived WAL allows point-in-time recovery, which is the only defence against mistakes that replication copies instantly.

useWhen: Use replicas for failover and to offload read-heavy, staleness-tolerant queries.
Use synchronous replication for data where losing acknowledged writes is unacceptable.
avoidWhen: Avoid sending read-after-write paths to async replicas without a consistency rule.
Avoid replacing backups with replicas.

rows: Writes stall if no sync standby is available

numbers.title: The latency cost of synchronous replication
assumptions: Primary and standby in different zones, 1.5 ms round trip (illustrative)
Local WAL flush 1 ms; standby flush 1 ms
steps: Async commit: about 1 ms (local flush).
Sync commit: local flush, then send, standby flush and confirm: about 1 + 1.5 + 1 = 3.5 ms (send and local flush can overlap, so often less).
A single client’s commit rate drops from about 1,000 to about 285 a second; concurrent clients still share flushes.
A standby in another region at 80 ms RTT would add 80 ms to every commit, which is why cross-region standbys are usually asynchronous.
numbers.result: Synchronous replication is cheap within a region and expensive across regions; choose per data set.

india.title: Replication options in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL high-availability chapter compares solutions including shared disk, file-system replication, WAL shipping, logical replication and synchronous multi-server setups, with a table of their trade-offs. The log-shipping chapter describes streaming replication, hot standby and synchronous standbys, and the continuous-archiving chapter describes point-in-time recovery from base backups and archived WAL, the safeguard that replication alone cannot provide.

Async replication can lose the lag window on failover; sync cannot, at a latency cost.
Plan read-your-writes for replica reads.
Replicas are not backups.

title: The NoSQL Families
objectives: Describe key-value, document, wide-column and graph databases
Model data around access patterns
Recognise when a relational database is still the better fit

cards.title: Different shapes for different questions
cards.body: “NoSQL” covers several data models. Key-value stores fetch a value by key. Document stores keep nested records, often JSON-like. Wide-column stores group rows by a partition key and sort them within it. Graph databases store nodes and relationships and follow links quickly.

cards.title: Worked example: designing a wide-column table from a query
cards.body: In wide-column stores, the table is shaped by the query it must answer.
steps: Assume: query “latest 20 messages in a chat”, run often; chats can have years of messages
Partition key: chat_id, so one chat’s messages live together
Clustering (sort) key: sent_at descending, so the newest come first
Partitions grow without bound, so add a time bucket: (chat_id, month)
cards.note: Result. Reading the latest 20 messages touches one partition and reads in sorted order. A different question, such as “all messages by one user”, needs a second table shaped for it, written alongside the first.

cards.title: Picking a family
cards.body: Start from the questions the application asks.
steps: Lookups by one id, no relationships: key-value
Self-contained records read and written whole: document
Huge write volume, reads by partition and range: wide-column
Many-hop relationship queries: graph
Ad-hoc queries, joins and multi-row transactions: relational

cards.title: Consistency and transactions vary
cards.body: Products differ in what they guarantee: some offer only single-key atomicity, others multi-document transactions; some let you choose per request between faster reads and reading the latest write. Check the guarantees of the product, not of the family.

cards.title: Trap: choosing NoSQL “for scale” before knowing the queries
cards.body: Models built around access patterns are fast for those patterns and awkward for new ones; adding a question can mean a new table and a backfill. If queries are still changing, a relational database (which also stores JSON and scales a long way) is often the safer start.

cards.title: Edge case: the partition key decides the hot spot
cards.body: Key-value and wide-column stores spread data by partition key. If many writes share one key, such as today’s date or a single popular tenant, they land on one partition and its limit becomes the whole system’s limit, however many nodes there are. Pick keys with many distinct, evenly used values, or add a suffix to spread a hot key.

questions.prompt: A session store needs “get session by id” and “delete session”, nothing else. Which family fits best?

choices.label: Graph

mechanism.title: How each family stores and queries data
steps: Key-value stores treat the value as opaque (or as a small data structure) and do only what the key allows: get, set, delete, often with expiry. In-memory ones are used for caches, sessions and counters; persistent ones for simple, very high-volume lookups.

Document stores hold nested records with flexible fields. You read and write a document as a unit, and can index fields inside it. The modelling question is what to embed (data read together) and what to reference (data shared or growing without bound).

Wide-column stores (in the style of Cassandra and Bigtable) distribute rows by partition key across nodes and sort them within a partition by clustering columns. Reads are efficient for one partition and a range within it; queries that cross partitions are expensive or not allowed, so tables are designed per query.
Graph databases store nodes and edges with properties and traverse relationships without join costs that grow with table size, which suits recommendations, fraud rings and network topologies.

Guarantees differ by product: atomicity per key, per document or across documents; tunable consistency levels; secondary-index support. Many systems favour availability and partition tolerance with eventual consistency, but several offer strong consistency options.

Relational databases now overlap heavily: JSON columns with indexes, partitioning, and distributed SQL systems. The choice is less “SQL vs NoSQL” and more which access patterns, guarantees and operational model you need.

useWhen: Use a NoSQL family when your access patterns are known and match its model.
Use more than one store when needs differ: a relational system of record plus a key-value cache, for example.
avoidWhen: Avoid choosing a store before you can list its queries.
Avoid unbounded partitions or documents that grow forever.

title: Schema Changes Without Downtime

cards.title: Schema changes are deployments
cards.body: A migration is a versioned script that moves the schema from one version to the next, kept in source control and applied the same way in every environment. On a live system, old and new application versions run side by side during a deploy, so every step must work with both.

cards.title: Worked example: backfilling a new column in batches
cards.body: Updating every row in one statement locks and bloats; batches keep each transaction short.
steps: Assume: 50 million rows; batches of 10,000 rows; each batch takes about 200 ms
Time: 5,000 × 0.2 s = 1,000 s ≈ 17 minutes, plus pauses
Each batch commits on its own, so locks are brief and replicas keep up
cards.note: Result. About 17 minutes of short transactions instead of one huge transaction holding locks on 50 million rows. Pausing between batches lets autovacuum and replicas keep pace.

cards.title: Expand and contract: renaming a column
cards.body: Never rename in place under a running app; move in compatible steps.
steps: Expand: add the new column
Deploy code that writes both columns and reads the old one
Backfill the new column in batches
Deploy code that reads the new column
Contract: stop writing the old column, then drop it

cards.title: Changes that lock or rewrite
cards.body: In PostgreSQL, adding a column with a constant default is fast (since version 11), but changing a column’s type usually rewrites the table under an exclusive lock. Plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not, though it takes longer and cannot run inside a transaction block. New constraints can be added as NOT VALID and validated later with a weaker lock.

cards.title: Trap: dropping a column the old code still reads
cards.body: During a rolling deploy some servers still run the previous version. If a migration drops or renames a column they use, those servers fail until the deploy finishes. Contract steps go in a later release, after no running code references the old column.

cards.title: Edge case: a quick ALTER that waits in line
cards.body: Even a fast schema change needs a brief exclusive lock. If a long-running query holds a conflicting lock, the ALTER waits, and every new query on that table queues behind the ALTER, so an “instant” migration takes the table offline. Set a short lock timeout on migrations (for example lock_timeout in PostgreSQL) and retry, instead of waiting indefinitely.

mechanism.title: How to change a schema under live traffic
steps: Migrations are numbered scripts applied in order, with a table in the database recording which have run. They are reviewed like code and are forward-only in production; undoing a change is a new migration, because data written after the change must be considered.

Rolling deploys mean old and new application versions overlap. Every migration step must be compatible with both: additive changes (new tables, nullable columns, new indexes) are safe; removals and renames are not, until no running code uses the old shape.

Expand and contract (also called parallel change) splits a breaking change into compatible steps: expand the schema, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then contract. Each step can be deployed and rolled back on its own.

Lock-sensitive operations: DDL takes table locks, and many ALTER TABLE forms take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Set lock_timeout so a migration gives up quickly instead of queueing every query behind it. Prefer operations that avoid rewrites: constant defaults, NOT VALID constraints followed by VALIDATE, concurrent index builds.

Some changes need a full rewrite (changing a column’s type in incompatible ways). Doing these online means building a new column or table, copying data in batches, keeping it in sync, then switching, which is expand and contract again.
Large data changes are run as background jobs, in batches by primary key range, with progress tracking and the ability to pause. Monitor replication lag and autovacuum while they run.

useWhen: Use additive migrations and expand and contract for anything that removes or renames.
Use lock timeouts and concurrent index builds on large, busy tables.
avoidWhen: Avoid editing migrations that have already run anywhere.
Avoid mixing large data backfills into the same transaction as schema changes.

rows: Add NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT

The table receives 300 writes a second
steps: A plain build blocks writes for the whole 20 minutes: 300 × 1,200 s = 360,000 writes waiting or failing.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY might take about twice as long, around 40 minutes, but writes continue throughout.
If a concurrent build fails, it leaves an invalid index that must be dropped and rebuilt.
Running it outside peak hours reduces its extra load on the table.
numbers.result: A longer, non-blocking change is almost always better than a short, blocking one on a live table.

The CREATE INDEX page describes building indexes concurrently, its extra cost, and that it cannot run inside a transaction block.

title: The N+1 Query Problem
objectives: Recognise the N+1 pattern from query logs
Rewrite it as a join or a batched query

cards.title: One query becomes many
cards.body: A page lists 50 posts, then for each post runs another query for its author. That is 1 query for the list plus N queries, one per row: N+1. Each is fast alone, but every one is a separate round trip, and the total grows with the page size.

cards.title: Worked example: 50 posts, 1 ms per round trip
cards.body: Round trips add up even when the database is quick.
steps: Assume: 50 posts, each query takes about 1 ms including the network round trip
N+1: 1 + 50 = 51 queries ≈ 51 ms
Batched: list query, then one query for all 50 authors by id ≈ 2 ms
Joined: one query returning posts with authors ≈ 1–2 ms
cards.note: Result. About 51 ms against about 2 ms under these assumptions. If the database is 5 ms away (another zone or region), N+1 becomes about 255 ms while the batched version stays near 10 ms.

cards.title: Fixing it with a batched query
cards.body: Collect the ids first, then fetch the related rows in one go.
steps: Query 1: SELECT the 50 posts
Collect their distinct author_ids
Query 2: SELECT authors WHERE id IN (… the ids …)
Match authors to posts in memory by id
Two round trips regardless of page size

cards.title: Where it hides
cards.body: Data-access layers that load related records lazily make N+1 easy to write by accident: the loop looks like it touches an object field, but each access runs a query. Templates and serialisers that read related fields per row are common culprits. Counting queries per request in logs or tests catches it.

cards.title: Trap: fixing N+1 with one huge join
cards.body: Joining several one-to-many relations at once (posts → comments → likes) multiplies rows and can return far more data than needed. Prefer a separate batched query per relation, which keeps results small and the number of queries constant.

cards.title: Edge case: batching with a huge IN list
cards.body: Fixing N+1 by loading related rows with WHERE id IN (...) works until the list holds tens of thousands of ids: statements get large, some drivers cap the number of bind parameters (PostgreSQL’s protocol allows at most 65,535), and plans change. Batch in chunks of a few hundred to a few thousand, or join against the parent query instead.

mechanism.title: Why N+1 hurts and how to remove it
steps: Every query pays a fixed cost: a network round trip, parsing or plan lookup, and scheduling on the server, before any rows are read. For tiny queries the fixed cost dominates, so many small queries are much slower than one query returning the same rows.
The N+1 pattern appears when code loops over a result and queries inside the loop. Its cost is (N + 1) × per-query cost, so it grows with page size and with network distance to the database.

Batching collects the ids from the first result and fetches all related rows at once with IN (…) or = ANY(array). The number of queries becomes constant: one per relation, independent of N. Very long id lists can be split into chunks of a few thousand.

Joins return parent and child data in one query. They are ideal for one-to-one and many-to-one relations (posts with their author). For one-to-many relations, a join repeats parent columns per child, so a separate batched query is often leaner.

Detection: log the number of queries per request, flag requests above a threshold, and add tests that assert query counts for key pages. Database statistics views that show the most frequently executed statements also reveal suspiciously high call counts.

When fetching in one query is impractical, pipelining (sending several queries without waiting for each result) or running independent queries in parallel reduces the round-trip cost, but batching usually removes the problem more simply.

useWhen: Use batched loads or joins whenever code fetches related data for a list.
Use query-count assertions in tests for important pages.
avoidWhen: Avoid queries inside loops over result sets.
Avoid joining several one-to-many relations at once, which multiplies rows.

rows: Grows with page size and distance

Cross region, N+1: 101 × 40 = 4,040 ms; batched: 2 × 40 = 80 ms.
The N+1 page goes from acceptable to unusable purely because of distance.
This is why moving an app or its database to another region often exposes hidden N+1 patterns.
numbers.result: N+1 multiplies network latency by the row count; batching makes the cost independent of it.

The documentation on row and array comparisons describes IN and = ANY, which batched loads rely on.

title: Connection Pooling
objectives: Explain why opening a database connection is expensive
Size a pool with Little’s law
Keep the total across many app instances under the server limit

cards.title: Connections are not free
cards.body: Opening a database connection means a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication and, in PostgreSQL, starting a server process for that connection. A pool keeps a set of open connections and lends one to each request for the duration of its queries, so that cost is paid once.

cards.title: Worked example: how many connections does the app need?
cards.body: Little’s law: connections in use = query rate × time each query holds a connection.
steps: Assume: 500 queries a second across the app, each holding a connection for 20 ms
In use on average: 500 × 0.020 = 10 connections
Allow headroom for bursts: a pool of 20
If queries slow to 60 ms under load: 500 × 0.060 = 30 in use, more than the pool
cards.note: Result. About 10 connections are busy on average, and a pool of 20 copes. If query time triples, requests start queueing for connections, so slow queries show up as pool waits in the application.

cards.title: Many instances, one database
cards.body: Every app instance has its own pool, and they all count against the server limit.
steps: The server allows 200 connections, with some reserved for admin
The app runs 30 instances with a pool of 10 each: 300
That exceeds the limit: new connections are refused
Shrink each pool, or put a shared pooler between the app and the database
Recheck whenever autoscaling adds instances

cards.title: Bigger is not faster
cards.body: A database has a fixed number of CPU cores and disks. Beyond a point, more concurrent queries just compete for them and for locks, and each gets slower. A smaller pool with a short queue in the app often gives better throughput and latency than hundreds of connections.

cards.title: Trap: session state with a transaction pooler
cards.body: A shared pooler in transaction mode gives each transaction whichever server connection is free. Session-level state (temporary tables, session settings, advisory locks, some prepared statement setups) does not follow you to the next transaction. Use session mode for code that needs it, or avoid session state.

cards.title: Edge case: pools multiplied by instances
cards.body: Each application instance has its own pool. Twenty instances with a pool of 20 each can open 400 connections, and autoscaling to 50 instances makes it 1,000, past the database’s max_connections. Size pools from the database’s limit divided by the maximum instance count, or put a shared pooler such as PgBouncer in front.

More concurrency than the database can run just adds contention.

mechanism.title: How pools work and how to size them
steps: In PostgreSQL each client connection is served by its own backend process, started when the client connects. Setup includes the network handshake, TLS if used, authentication, and process start, which together cost far more than a typical indexed query.

A pool keeps connections open and lends them out. Requests borrow a connection, run their queries or transaction, and return it. Pools usually have a maximum size, a minimum idle count, a wait timeout for borrowers, and a maximum lifetime so connections are recycled.

Little’s law gives the average number in use: arrival rate × hold time. Hold time includes everything done while holding the connection, so code that does network calls or heavy computation in the middle of a transaction inflates it.

The server has a hard limit (max_connections, 100 by default in PostgreSQL, with a few slots reserved for superusers), and each connection uses memory. The sum of all pools across instances, jobs, migrations and admin tools must fit under it.

External poolers sit between many app instances and the database, multiplexing thousands of client connections onto a small set of server connections. In transaction mode a server connection is assigned per transaction, which is efficient but breaks session-level state.

Throughput peaks at a modest number of active connections, related to the database’s cores and storage; beyond that, contention for CPU, locks and I/O raises latency. Measure with realistic load to find the point, rather than raising pool sizes when things are slow.

useWhen: Use a pool in every long-running service that talks to a database.
Size pools from Little’s law plus headroom, and budget totals across all instances.
avoidWhen: Avoid opening a connection per request.
Avoid holding a connection while waiting on slow external calls.

numbers.title: What happens when queries slow down
assumptions: Pool of 20; 400 queries a second (illustrative)
Normal hold time 25 ms; during an incident it rises to 80 ms
steps: Normal: 400 × 0.025 = 10 busy, half the pool.
Incident: 400 × 0.080 = 32 needed, more than the 20 available.
Requests queue for connections; if the pool wait timeout is 1 s, some start failing even though the database is up.
Raising the pool to 40 only adds load to a database that is already slow; fixing the slow query (or shedding load) restores the margin.
numbers.result: Pool exhaustion is usually a symptom of slower queries; Little’s law shows how quickly a small slowdown uses up the headroom.

india.title: Connections in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: PostgreSQL’s documentation explains that the server starts a separate backend process for each connection (“process per user”), and the max_connections setting defaults to 100 connections, with some reserved for superusers. The kernel-resources chapter shows how connection counts drive memory and semaphore needs, which is why large numbers of idle connections are costly even when they do nothing.

pitfalls.say: “Hold times probably rose; I’d find the slow queries first, since a bigger pool adds load to a struggling database.”

pitfalls.trap: “Each instance has a small pool, so we’re fine.”
pitfalls.say: “Instances times pool size must fit under max_connections; autoscaling can blow through it.”

takeaways: Opening connections is expensive; pools reuse them.
Busy connections = query rate × hold time.
Sum of pools across instances must fit the server limit.
Bigger pools past the database’s capacity add contention.

interactive.title: Size the pool
interactive.prompt: Your app sends 500 queries a second through a pool of 20 connections. Slide how long each query holds its connection.
interactive.takeaway: At 20 ms about 10 connections are busy. Once queries hold a connection for 40 ms or more, all 20 are busy and requests queue. Slower queries, not more traffic, are the usual reason pools run dry.

seeAlso.why: Scaling app servers horizontally
Ports and sockets are what a connection pool holds open
